questions.question: Two fraction bars are exactly the same size, and one whole bar is one whole. Each bar is cut into 4 equal parts. All 4 parts of the first bar are shaded, and 3 of the 4 parts of the second bar are shaded. Which mixed number names the total shaded amount?
questions.explain: The first bar is 4/4, which is 1 whole, and 3 more fourths are shaded, so the amount is 1 3/4. The big trap is squeezing the digits together as 13/4 — a mixed number is ONE number, meaning 1 whole plus 3 fourths, not the two numbers 1 and 3 sitting side by side.

questions.question: Three identical fraction bars are each cut into 3 equal parts, and one whole bar is one whole. Both of the first two bars are completely shaded, and 1 part of the third bar is shaded. Which improper fraction tells how much is shaded in all?
questions.explain: Count every shaded piece in thirds: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 thirds, so the improper fraction is 7/3. The denominator stays 3 because 3 equal parts make ONE whole — it does not turn into 9 just because 9 parts were drawn altogether.

questions.question: Two identical fraction bars are each cut into 5 equal parts, and one whole bar is one whole. All 5 parts of the first bar are shaded, and 2 parts of the second bar are shaded. Which choice names the shaded amount correctly?
options: 7/10, because 10 parts were drawn in all
7/5, which is the same as 12/5
7/5, which is the same as 1 2/5
2/5, because only the second bar counts
questions.explain: Five fifths fill the first bar and 2 more fifths are shaded, so 7 fifths, or 7/5, are shaded, and that is 1 whole plus 2/5, written 1 2/5. Watch out: 1 2/5 must never be written as 12/5 — the 1 and the 2/5 are joined into one number, not printed next to each other.

questions.question: Three identical fraction bars are each cut into 6 equal parts, and one whole bar is one whole. The first two bars are fully shaded, and 5 of the 6 parts of the third bar are shaded. Which mixed number names the shaded amount?
questions.explain: Two bars are completely shaded, which is 2 wholes, and 5 more sixths are shaded, so the amount is 2 5/6 (the same as 17/6). Writing it as 25/6 is the classic mistake — that reads as twenty-five sixths, which is over 4 wholes, not 2 wholes and a bit.

questions.question: Write the mixed number 2 3/5 as an improper fraction.
questions.explain: Change the 2 wholes into fifths first: 2 x 5 = 10 fifths, then add the extra 3 fifths to get 13/5. The most common error is writing the digits side by side as 23/5, which treats the 2 and the 3/5 as two separate numbers instead of one amount.

questions.question: Which choice correctly writes the improper fraction 11/4 as a mixed number?
questions.explain: Ask how many groups of 4 fourths fit in 11 fourths: 11 divided by 4 is 2 with 3 left over, so 11/4 = 2 3/4, and the denominator stays 4. Careful with the leftovers — the 2 is the number of wholes and the 3 is the number of fourths left, and squashing them into 23/4 changes the number completely.

questions.question: At a school bake sale in Burnaby, each pan of apple crisp is cut into 8 equal pieces. Noor's class eats 19 pieces. Written as a mixed number, how many pans of apple crisp did they eat?
options: 3 2/8 pans
23/8 pans
2 3/8 pans
2 3/19 pans
questions.explain: Eight pieces make one full pan, so 19 pieces is 8 + 8 + 3, which is 2 full pans and 3 pieces left, or 2 3/8 pans. The trap is writing that as 23/8 — the whole number and the fraction join into one value, they are not two numbers printed together.

questions.question: Ella needs to change 4 1/3 into an improper fraction. Which method actually works?
options: Put the 4 in front of the 1 to get 41/3
Add 4 + 1 + 3 and write the total over 3, giving 8/3
Multiply 4 x 3 and write it over 3, giving 12/3
Multiply 4 x 3 to get 12 thirds, add the 1 extra third, and keep 3 as the denominator, giving 13/3
questions.explain: Each whole is 3 thirds, so 4 wholes are 4 x 3 = 12 thirds, and the extra third makes 13/3. Sliding the 4 in front of the 1 to make 41/3 is the classic slip: 4 1/3 is one number, a bit more than 4, while 41/3 is close to 14.

questions.question: Ravi's running route is shown on a number line from 0 km to 3 km, and every kilometre is split into 4 equal parts. His water station is at the tick mark 3 spaces to the right of 1 km. Which choice names that spot both ways?
options: 7/4 km and 1 3/4 km
3/4 km and 0 3/4 km
7/4 km and 13/4 km
7/12 km and 1 3/4 km
questions.explain: Count the fourths from 0: four of them reach 1 km, and 3 more land on the station, so it is 7/4 km, which is 1 whole kilometre plus 3/4, written 1 3/4 km. Remember the denominator counts the parts in ONE kilometre, and 1 3/4 can never be squashed into 13/4, which would sit past 3 km.

questions.question: Noah measured 3 1/2 litres of water for a science experiment, but in his notebook he wrote it as 31/2 L. Which statement explains what went wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: 3 1/2 is just the number 3 beside the number 1/2, so 31/2 says the same thing
It is wrong because 3 1/2 means 3 wholes plus 1 half, which is 7/2 L, while 31/2 L would be more than 15 L
It is wrong because 3 1/2 should be written as 3/2 L
It is wrong because 3 1/2 should be written as 4/2 L
questions.explain: Turn the wholes into halves: 3 x 2 = 6 halves plus 1 half is 7/2, so 3 1/2 L = 7/2 L. The mistake to avoid is reading a mixed number as two separate numbers stuck together, because 31/2 means thirty-one halves, over 15 litres.

questions.question: At a Surrey bake sale, every banana loaf is cut into 4 equal slices. One family eats 2 whole loaves and 1 extra slice. Which choice names the amount they ate?
options: 9/12 loaves, which is 3/4 of a loaf
9/4 loaves, which is 21/4 loaves
9/4 loaves, which is 2 1/4 loaves
4/9 loaves, which is less than 1 loaf
questions.explain: First count the slices in quarters: 2 loaves are 4 + 4 = 8 slices, plus 1 more slice is 9 slices, so 9/4 loaves, and 9/4 regroups into 2 wholes with 1 quarter left, or 2 1/4 loaves. Writing that as 21/4 is the usual trap — it would mean twenty-one quarters, over 5 loaves.

questions.question: Owen is marking 1 4/5 on a number line that runs from 0 to 5, with each whole split into 5 equal parts. He says, 'The 1 and the 4/5 are two numbers, so I will put it between 4 and 5.' Where does 1 4/5 really belong, and why?
options: Between 0 and 1, because 4/5 is less than one whole
Exactly at 5, because 1 + 4 = 5
Between 4 and 5, because the 4 and the 5 are the numbers to look at
Between 1 and 2, because it means 1 whole plus 4 more fifths, which is 9/5
questions.explain: A mixed number is one whole number plus a fraction of the next whole, so 1 4/5 starts at 1 and moves 4 fifths further, landing just before 2 (it equals 9/5). The trap Owen fell into is treating the whole number and the fraction as separate numbers to read off — they describe one single point.
